newsitem.title: USA: CSCE, NYCE say agree to discuss merger.
newsitem.headline: CSCE, NYCE say agree to discuss merger.

text.p: The Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange and the New York Cotton Exchange said Thursday they agreed to explore a possible merger in a move that appeared to end years of speculation over the future of the two exchanges.

"The Boards of the Coffee, Sugar & Cocoa Exchange Inc. (CSCE) and New York Cotton Exchange (NYCE) have agreed to explore the feasibility of developing a proposal by which the two exchanges could enter into a merger that would be equitable to the members of both exchanges," the commodity exchanges said in a statement.
The chairmen and presidents of both New York-based exchanges were instructed by their respective boards to develop a merger proposal, the statement said.
No further details of the merger were provided.

The coffee exchange trades futures and options contracts in coffee, cocoa, sugar and dairy products. The cotton exchange trades futures and options contracts in cotton, orange juice and financial futures including the U.S. Dollar Index, Treasury notes and U.S.-based currency contracts.
Joe O'Neill, president of the cotton exchange, said in an interview that the boards of both exchanges had met separately on Thursday to vote on the proposal.
No date has been set for a meeting to begin developing a merger agreement, he said.

The two exchanges have said they plan to build a joint trading facility in lower Manhattan in New York City. Last year coffee exchange President Jim Bowe said the exchanges were exploring ways to consolidate their operations, including the possibility of a merger.
Asked if the exchanges were going ahead with the construction of a new trading facility, O'Neill said no work had begun on a new site.
"We're still talking to NYMEX about moving into their facility with them," he added, referring to the New York Mercantile Exchange's plans to move into new state-of-the-art quarters early next month.
A spokesman for the coffee exchange declined further comment.

Questions about whether the coffee and cotton exchanges would agree to join forces have swirled since the two exchanges announced in 1995 that they would relocate across the Hudson River to New Jersey. That plan was abandoned when the New York City and New York State offered the exchanges an incentive package worth some $90 million to stay in Manhattan.

At that time, the New York Mercantile Exchange approached the coffee exchange with a merger bid valued at nearly $50 million. The deal, which was rejected by the coffee exchange, did not include the cotton exchange.
The proposed link-up of the two exchange comes at a time of increasing consolidation among the world's commodity exchanges.

In 1994, the New York Mercantile Exchange acquired the Commodity Exchange (COMEX), while last year's merger between the London Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) and and the London Commodities Exchange quashed a bid by New York's coffee exchange to acquire its British rival.
